claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC state.
The range of phases formed during cooling and thermal exposure originates from thermally activated local chemical-ordering instabilities.
Local chemical-ordering instabilities occur within the initial high-temperature BCC phase.
These ordering instabilities promote heterogeneous nucleation of ordered B2 or other intermetallic-like nanodomains.
Ordered nanodomains subsequently grow into distinct secondary phases during thermal exposure.
Cooling with only limited atomic diffusion produces a metastable BCC state.
Intermediate-temperature thermal exposure activates diffusion and atomic rearrangement without fully re-equilibrating the parent BCC structure.
Extreme rapid quenching or exposure where diffusion remains frozen prevents ordered-phase nucleation.
Local chemical ordering and compositional fluctuations are concentrated at grain boundaries and within sub-grain regions.
Localized compositional fluctuations formed during cooling generate incipient ordered clusters.
Thermally activated diffusion accelerates the growth and coarsening of ordered clusters.
The transformation is governed by competition between thermodynamic ordering forces and kinetic barriers to diffusion.
Slow cooling or isothermal holds during cooling produce a higher volume fraction of ordered secondary phases than rapid cooling.
The secondary ordered phases have lattice symmetries distinguishable from the BCC parent phase.
Rapidly cooled samples with minimal thermal exposure remain predominantly homogeneous metastable BCC.
Intermediate-temperature exposure produces nanoscale-ordering evolution detectable by TEM and XRD.
Exposures below or above the proposed activation window do not produce the same phase diversity.
Sufficiently high thermal-exposure temperatures can completely homogenize the alloy or dissolve or melt incipient ordered clusters.
Thermal evolution of local chemical order and phase-boundary configurations can affect the mechanical behavior of a eutectic high-entropy alloy.
High-entropy-alloy microstructures can contain nanoprecipitates, ordered and disordered solid-solution phases, and amorphous phases.
